new_statements.quote: Both Wapishana and Mawayana have intensity stress, placed on the penultimate mora of a phonological word (i.e., if the final syllable is CV, then the penultimate syllable is stressed; if the final syllable is CVC or CVV, the final syllable is stressed; [...]). [p. 73] [...] In Mawayana, in contrast, secondary stress falls on even-numbered CV syllables from the beginning to the end of the word (/wa-katuku-sɨ/ [wa.ˌkaː.tu.ˈkuː.sɨ] ‘our club, stick’); non-CV syllables are always stressed (/awjaɗa/ [ˈaw.ja.ɗa] ‘toucan sp.’). Unlike Wapishana, Mawayana stress is thus sensitive to prefixes, not suffixes (e.g., /kanawa/ [ka.ˈnaː.wa] ‘canoe’, /wa-kanawa/ [wa.ˈkaː.na.wa] ‘our canoe’). Stressed vowels are usually lengthened; unstressed vowels, though unlengthened, do not reduce or disappear [p. 74]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Mawayana has a left-to-right rhythmic (Cariban-type) stress system: counting from the beginning of the phonological word, every even-numbered CV syllable is stressed; heavy (non-CV: CVV, CVN) syllables are always stressed; stressed vowels lengthen. The author's general statement puts primary stress on the penultimate mora (penult if the final syllable is CV, final if it is CVC/CVV), but his Mawayana examples put primary stress on the rightmost non-final rhythmic stress ([ka.ˈnaː.wa] 'canoe' vs. [wa.ˈkaː.na.wa] 'our canoe', [wa.ˌkaː.tu.ˈkuː.sɨ]), so primary position depends on syllable count and weight from the left, and prefixes shift it. In Sec. 7 (p. 80) Meira argues this pattern is borrowed from Cariban (Waiwai/Tiriyó), Wapishana's right-to-left system being original.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on even-numbered CV syllables counting from the beginning of the word; non-CV syllables always stressed (Wapishana, by contrast, counts backwards from the primary stress).
new_statements.exceptions: The two statements on pp. 73–74 are in tension: the 'penultimate mora' generalisation is stated for both languages, but /wa-kanawa/ [wa.ˈkaː.na.wa] shows primary stress on the second syllable, not the penult. Diphthongs/long vowels are 'always stressed on the first vowel'. Stress of word-initial syllabic nasals (/n.taɾu/) not discussed.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (prefix + stem + suffix, e.g. /wa-katuku-sɨ/); based on elicited words/sentences and a short text from 1–2 elderly speakers (Meira's 1997 Mapuera data, Howard's 1985-86 questionnaire, Carlin's Suriname text). This is a comparative-historical article with a first-hand phonology summary, not a dedicated phonological description; Coretta 2013 (unseen) would supersede it.
new_statements.identity_note: mawa1271 (Mawayana, mzx) is a retired Glottolog entry; Glottolog merged it into Mapidian-Mawayana [mapi1252, ISO mpw] on the evidence of Howard 2001 that the ethnonyms denote the same group. All sources found describe Mawayana as spoken by the last speakers living in Waiwai villages (Mapuera, Pará; Kaxmi, Roraima) and in Kwamalasamutu, Suriname; the stress statement (Meira 2019) rests on his own 1997 field data from a Mapuera speaker plus Howard 1985-86 and Carlin's Suriname data. Catalog it under mapi1252 / mpw with 'Mawayana' as the variety name.
